title: Trigonometry
summary: Ratios, the standard-value table, the three identities, complementary angles, value-putting and max-min values. Tier 1 reliably holds 2-4 trig questions and they fall almost mechanically to the value table, one identity, or a 3-4-5 style triangle — among the cheapest marks in the paper.

subtopics.title: Ratios and standard values
subtopics.concept:
For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right triangle: $\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$,
$\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$, and
$\text{cosec}=\frac1{\sin}$, $\sec=\frac1{\cos}$, $\cot=\frac1{\tan}$.

**Standard value table (memorise cold — most CGL questions are one lookup away):**

| $\theta$ | $0^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin$ | $0$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $\cos$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\frac12$ | $0$ |
| $\tan$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | undef. |

tricks.title: The 1-2-3 memory trick for sin
tricks.body:
Write $\frac{\sqrt0}{2},\frac{\sqrt1}{2},\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac{\sqrt4}{2}$ for
$0^\circ,30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ,90^\circ$ — the sin row falls out; the cos row is the same read backwards.
Divide the two rows to get tan.

tricks.title: Reciprocal first, table second
tricks.body: When an expression has cosec/sec/cot, flip each to sin/cos/tan before touching the table.

mistakes: $\tan90^\circ$ treated as $0$ or $1$ — it is undefined.
Reciprocal flipped the wrong way ($\sec\theta$ taken as $\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$).
subtopics.notes:
### The standard-value table (build it, don't memorise it)
$$\sin: \frac{\sqrt0}{2}, \frac{\sqrt1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \frac{\sqrt4}{2} \text{ at } 0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$$
cos is the same list read backwards; tan = sin/cos gives $0, \frac{1}{\sqrt3}, 1, \sqrt3, \infty$. Then reciprocals give cosec, sec, cot. The $\frac{\sqrt{k}}{2}$ construction means the table can never be forgotten under pressure.

### One ratio → the whole triangle
Any single ratio pins the triangle's SHAPE: draw a right triangle with sides in that ratio, get the third side by Pythagoras, read off every other ratio.
- $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ → sides 3-4-5 → $\tan\theta = \frac34$.
- $\cos\theta = \frac{12}{13}$ → 5-12-13 → $\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}$, $\tan\theta = \frac{5}{12}$.
- $\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt7}$ → hyp $\sqrt{1+7} = 2\sqrt2$ → $\cosec\theta = 2\sqrt2$.
Keep ratios as fractions to the end; rationalise only the final answer if options are surd-free.

### Two sides → every ratio
Given two sides of the right triangle: third side first (Pythagoras), then name the angle carefully — the ratio asked is relative to a SPECIFIC acute angle: opposite/hyp for its sine, adjacent/hyp for its cosine. "The smaller angle" sits opposite the shorter leg. Triangles 5-12-13, 7-24-25, 8-15-17, 9-40-41 and their multiples supply almost all exam numbers.

### Combining ratios safely
When an expression mixes functions ($\sec 60^\circ + \cosec 30^\circ$, $\cot 30^\circ + \tan 60^\circ$), reduce each term to the $\sin$/$\cos$ table values first, then add — do not invent product rules. The angle-difference formula $\tan(A - B) = \frac{\tan A - \tan B}{1 + \tan A \tan B}$ occasionally appears disguised as a pure 60/30 evaluation; recognising it turns a messy fraction into $\tan 30^\circ$.

### The reciprocal rows (never leave home without them)
Flip the main table for the rest: $\cosec 30^\circ = 2$, $\cosec 45^\circ = \sqrt2$, $\cosec 60^\circ = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}$; $\sec 60^\circ = 2$, $\sec 45^\circ = \sqrt2$, $\sec 30^\circ = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ (sec runs opposite to cosec); $\cot 30^\circ = \sqrt3$, $\cot 45^\circ = 1$, $\cot 60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ — cot is tan read backwards. Expressions like $\cosec^2 30^\circ + \sec^2 45^\circ$ are then pure table work: $4 + 2 = 6$. Spot the reciprocal twins that cancel: $\cosec 30^\circ - \sec 60^\circ = 2 - 2 = 0$ and $\tan 30^\circ \tan 60^\circ = 1$.

### Quick revision
- $\sin$ column $\frac{\sqrt{0,1,2,3,4}}{2}$; cos reversed; tan $= \frac{\sin}{\cos}$.
- One ratio → 3-4-5 / 5-12-13 / 7-24-25 triangle → all ratios.
- Smaller acute angle ⟷ shorter opposite leg.
- $\tan(60^\circ - 30^\circ)$ identity rescues $\frac{\tan A - \tan B}{1+\tan A\tan B}$ expressions.

patterns.name: Standard values at 0/30/45/60/90
patterns.howToSpot: A sum/difference of ratios at special angles asked directly.
patterns.formula: Read each term off the $\frac{\sqrt{k}}{2}$ table; add last.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert every function to its table value (sec/cot too — reciprocals of the cos/tan rows).
2. Keep surds as surds; add only matching radicals.
3. Rationalise only at the very end if options demand it.

Why: each term is a fixed constant — the question only tests retrieval plus one line of arithmetic.

example.solution: $\frac12 + \frac12 = 1$. Both are the table's middle entries.

patterns.name: One given ratio → the other ratios
patterns.howToSpot: 'If sinθ = 3/5, find tanθ' — one ratio given (sometimes in a surd form), others asked.
patterns.formula: Construct the 3-4-5 (or matching) triangle; read the asked ratio off it.
patterns.logic:
1. Write opp/adj from the given ratio; complete the triangle with Pythagoras.
2. Read the asked ratio; rationalise surds at the end.
3. Sign checks are unnecessary for acute exam angles — everything positive.

Why: one ratio fixes the shape, so every other ratio is a re-reading of the same triangle.

example.q: If $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:

patterns.name: Two sides of the triangle → ratios
patterns.howToSpot: Two sides of a right triangle given (or hyp + one side); a named ratio of one acute angle asked.
patterns.formula: Third side by Pythagoras, then $\sin = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\cos = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$ w.r.t. the NAMED angle.
patterns.logic:
1. Complete the triangle (5-12-13, 7-24-25, 8-15-17 multiples).
2. Identify the angle: 'opposite the shorter leg' = smaller angle.
3. Opposite/adjacent w.r.t. that angle — the top exam trap is flipping them.

Why: the triangle is fully determined; only the naming of the angle can go wrong.

example.q: In a triangle right-angled at B, AB = 5 cm and BC = 12 cm. The value of sin A is:
example.solution: AC $= 13$; $\sin A = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}} = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{12}{13}$. Note the opposite side to A is BC, not AB.

patterns.name: Mixed-function combinations
patterns.howToSpot: Expressions mixing sec, cosec, cot at special angles — or a tan-difference formula hidden inside a fraction.
patterns.formula: Reciprocal table entries; $\tan(A-B) = \frac{\tan A - \tan B}{1 + \tan A\tan B}$ rescues the disguised ones.
patterns.logic:
1. Replace sec/cosec/cot by reciprocals of table values.
2. If the expression matches $\frac{\tan A - \tan B}{1 + \tan A \tan B}$, rewrite as $\tan(A - B)$ and read the table once.
3. Compare with the options in surd form first; rationalise only if needed.

Why: the fraction pattern is invisible until you look for it — that's the entire difficulty of these questions.

subtopics.title: Fundamental identities
subtopics.concept:
Three identities drive almost every simplification:
$$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,\qquad 1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta,\qquad 1+\cot^2\theta=\text{cosec}^2\theta$$
Each splits into handy parts: $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$, $\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1$,
$\text{cosec}^2\theta-\cot^2\theta=1$. Expressions with $\sin^6+\cos^6$ or $\sin^4+\cos^4$ reduce through
these — treat $x=\sin^2\theta$ so $x+(1-x)=1$.

tricks.title: Substitute $x=\sin^2\theta$
tricks.body: Everything above degree 4 collapses with $x$ and $1-x$. Memorise the two reduced forms for 4th and 6th powers.

tricks.title: Sec/tan pairs move as one
tricks.body:
See $\sec^2$ and $\tan^2$ together → replace by 1 (or by each other via $\sec^2=1+\tan^2$). Same for
cosec/cot.

mistakes: Expanding $\sin^6+\cos^6$ as $(\sin^2+\cos^2)^3$ without subtracting the cross terms.
subtopics.notes:
### The three identity engines
$$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1,\qquad 1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta,\qquad 1 + \cot^2\theta = \cosec^2\theta$$
Every identity question runs one of three engines:
1. **Divide by $\cos^2$** (or $\sin^2$): $\frac{\sin^2}{\cos^2} + 1 = \frac{1}{\cos^2}$ is the second identity — so any $\sec^2 \pm \tan^2$ combination converts to a single ratio.
2. **Pair products**: $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)(\sec\theta - \tan\theta) = 1$, $(\cosec\theta + \cot\theta)(\cosec\theta - \cot\theta) = 1$ — conjugate pairs whose product is 1.
3. **Squares of sums**: $(\sin\theta \pm \cos\theta)^2 = 1 \pm 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ — links "sin+cos = m" questions to "sin·cos" questions.

### The sin+cos / sin−cos web
Given $\sin\theta + \cos\theta = m$: squaring gives $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{m^2 - 1}{2}$, and $(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 = 2 - m^2$. Given $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = m$, the conjugate gives $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac1m$ — then adding/subtracting the pair returns $\sec\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ individually (this 2-step unlocks $\sin\theta$ via a triangle).

### Convert-to-sin-cos for anything composite
For fractions mixing tan/sin/cos with an unknown coefficient ("if $\tan\theta = \frac34$, find $\frac{4\sin\theta - \cos\theta}{4\cos\theta + \sin\theta}$"): divide numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$ — everything becomes $t = \tan\theta$, one substitution, one fraction. Squared combos like $\tan^2\theta + \cot^2\theta$ come from squaring $\tan\theta + \cot\theta$ and subtracting 2.

### The fourth- and sixth-power chains
Two reduced forms answer a whole question family:
$$\sin^4\theta + \cos^4\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta, \qquad \sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta = 1 - 3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$$
Both come from squaring/cubing $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$. The classic combination $2(\sin^6 + \cos^6) - 3(\sin^4 + \cos^4) + 1$ then collapses: $2 - 6s^2c^2 - 3 + 6s^2c^2 + 1 = 0$ for every $\theta$ — the cross terms cancel by design. When a question mixes powers, reduce each bracket to these two forms first and only then simplify; almost always the $s^2c^2$ terms cancel and a constant survives.

### Quick revision
- $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$; divide it by $\cos^2$ or $\sin^2$ for the other two.
- $(\sec + \tan)(\sec - \tan) = 1$; same for cosec/cot.
- $(\sin \pm \cos)^2 = 1 \pm 2\sin\cos$; $\sin\cos = \frac{(\sin+\cos)^2 - 1}{2}$.
- Composite fractions: divide top and bottom by $\cos\theta$.
- $\tan\theta + \cot\theta = \sec\theta\,\cosec\theta$; squaring then subtracting 2 gives the squared sum.

patterns.name: Conjugate pairs: sec±tan, cosec±cot
patterns.howToSpot: 'If secθ + tanθ = m, find secθ − tanθ' (or the reverse) — or the pair used to extract individual ratios.
patterns.formula: (\sec\theta + \tan\theta)(\sec\theta - \tan\theta) = 1
patterns.logic:
1. The conjugate is its reciprocal: $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac1m$.
2. To extract $\tan\theta$: subtract the pair ($2\tan\theta = m - \frac1m$).
3. Then a 3-4-5 style triangle gives sin/cos if asked.

Why: the product being exactly 1 makes every question in this family a two-line reciprocal computation.

example.q: If $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 5$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta - \tan\theta$ is:

patterns.name: sin²+cos² expansions and squares of sums
patterns.howToSpot: Expressions like (sinθ ± cosθ)², or a product like (cosecθ − sinθ)(secθ − cosθ)(tanθ + cotθ) to simplify.
patterns.formula: (\sin\theta \pm \cos\theta)^2 = 1 \pm 2\sin\theta\cos\theta; convert everything to sin/cos and cancel.
patterns.logic:
1. Expand squares: the cross term $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and the 1 dominate.
2. For composite products, convert each bracket to sin/cos: $\cosec\theta - \sin\theta = \frac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta}$ etc., then cancel.
3. Constants fall out — most of these expressions are pure numbers (1 or 2).

Why: every term is secretly $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ wearing a costume.

patterns.name: Substituting tan via divide-by-cos
patterns.howToSpot: tanθ given; a linear fraction in sinθ and cosθ asked — coefficients on both.
patterns.formula: Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$; the fraction becomes one in $t = \tan\theta$.
patterns.logic:
1. $\frac{a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta}{c\cos\theta + d\sin\theta} = \frac{a\tan\theta + b}{c + d\tan\theta}$.
2. Substitute $t$; simplify the single fraction.
3. Keep fractions exact ($t = \frac34$, not 0.75).

Why: division by $\cos\theta$ is legal (nonzero for acute angles) and converts two unknowns into one.

patterns.name: Squared sums via squaring (tan+cot, sin+cosec)
patterns.howToSpot: 'If tanθ + cotθ = k, find tan²θ + cot²θ' — or an equation like sinθ + cosecθ = 2 that forces a special value.
patterns.formula: Square the given: $(x + \frac{1}{x})^2 = x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2} + 2$, so subtract 2. Equations equal to 2 force $x = 1$.
patterns.logic:
1. Square the given sum; subtract 2 for the squared-pair answer.
2. AM-GM shortcut: $x + \frac1x \ge 2$, with equality only at $x = 1$ — so "= 2" means $\tan\theta = \sin\theta = 1$, i.e. $\theta = 45^\circ$ / $90^\circ$ respectively.
3. Read off the asked power exactly (squared vs fourth).

Why: the self-reciprocal structure makes both the bound and the equality case immediate.

example.q: If $\tan\theta + \cot\theta = 5$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan^2\theta + \cot^2\theta$ is:

subtopics.title: Complementary angles
subtopics.concept:
For angles that add to $90^\circ$:
$$\sin(90^\circ-\theta)=\cos\theta,\quad \tan(90^\circ-\theta)=\cot\theta,\quad \sec(90^\circ-\theta)=\text{cosec}\theta$$
and similarly in reverse. This converts "odd" angles ($67\tfrac12^\circ$, $72^\circ$, ...) into their partners and
makes paired products equal 1: $\tan\theta\cdot\tan(90^\circ-\theta)=1$.

An equation like $\sin(A+\theta)=\cos(B+\theta)$ forces $(A+\theta)+(B+\theta)=90^\circ$.

tricks.title: Pair the angles that add to 90°
tricks.body:
In a long product, look for $\theta$ and $90-\theta$ pairs first — each pair collapses to 1. The classic
$\tan1^\circ\tan2^\circ\cdots\tan89^\circ$ collapses completely.

tricks.title: Convert everything to one angle
tricks.body:
Rewrite each term at its complementary partner until only one angle remains; a $\sin^2+\cos^2$ pair may then
collapse.

tricks.title: Equation → sum to 90°
tricks.body: When $\sin(\ldots)=\cos(\ldots)$, set the two bracketed angles to sum to $90^\circ$ and solve.

example.q: If $\sin(40^\circ+\theta)=\cos(30^\circ+\theta)$ and both angles are acute, find $\theta$.

mistakes: Complementary conversion applied to the wrong function ($\sec(90-\theta)=\sec\theta$ is wrong).
Setting $\sin A=\cos B\Rightarrow A+B=180^\circ$ — it is $90^\circ$.
Products paired as $\tan\theta\cdot\cot\theta=1$ but evaluated before converting to the same angle.
subtopics.notes:
### The complementary pair rules
For any angle $\theta$: $\sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta$, $\tan(90^\circ - \theta) = \cot\theta$, $\sec(90^\circ - \theta) = \cosec\theta$ — and each reversed. The switch only happens between the three PAIRS (sin↔cos, tan↔cot, sec↔cosec); sin to sin at $90^\circ - \theta$ never changes function.
$$\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ - \theta),\quad \tan\theta = \cot(90^\circ - \theta),\quad \sec\theta = \cosec(90^\circ - \theta)$$

### The working algorithm
1. Scan the expression for angles that sum to $90^\circ$ in pairs ($20^\circ$ & $70^\circ$, $35^\circ$ & $55^\circ$, $5^\circ$ & $85^\circ$...).
2. Convert ONE angle of each pair so both terms share an angle: $\sec 55^\circ = \cosec 35^\circ = \frac{1}{\sin 35^\circ}$.
3. Fractions collapse ($x \cdot \frac1x$), products of the form $\tan\theta\cot\theta$ become 1, and the expression evaluates to a small constant.

### Product chains
Products like $\tan 5^\circ \tan 25^\circ \tan 45^\circ \tan 65^\circ \tan 85^\circ$ pair into $\tan\theta \cdot \tan(90^\circ - \theta) = \tan\theta\cot\theta = 1$ with $\tan 45^\circ = 1$ left over. The full run $\tan 1^\circ \tan 2^\circ \cdots \tan 89^\circ$ is 1 for the same reason — 44 cancelling pairs around the middle term.

### Finding the angle itself
Equations pairing different functions at related angles resolve by forcing the SAME function: $\sin 3A = \cos(A - 10^\circ)$ becomes $\sin 3A = \sin(90^\circ - (A - 10^\circ))$, so the angles match: $3A = 100^\circ - A$. Equivalently, complementary-function arguments must sum to $90^\circ$: $\sec 2\theta = \cosec(\theta + 30^\circ)$ gives $2\theta + \theta + 30^\circ = 90^\circ$.

### The tan 45° anchor and half-chain variants
$\tan 45^\circ = 1$ is the middle term of every full chain and the most common "unpaired" value in short products. Half-chains behave the same: $\tan 10^\circ \tan 20^\circ \tan 70^\circ \tan 80^\circ = (10,80)(20,70) = 1$, and cot chains like $\cot 15^\circ \cot 35^\circ \cot 55^\circ \cot 75^\circ$ collapse identically because complementary cots are still reciprocals. One caution: the collapse needs PAIRS summing to $90^\circ$ — if a product holds $\tan 20^\circ \tan 50^\circ \tan 40^\circ$, the $20/70$ pairing is absent, so convert through cot and simplify before trusting a pattern.

### Quick revision
- Only three switches exist: sin↔cos, tan↔cot, sec↔cosec, argument → $90^\circ - x$.
- Hunt pairs summing to $90^\circ$; convert, then cancel.
- $\tan\theta \cdot \tan(90^\circ - \theta) = 1$; full chains $\tan 1^\circ \cdots \tan 89^\circ = 1$.
- Angle equations: set complementary arguments to sum to $90^\circ$, solve linearly.

patterns.name: Pair conversion to collapse a sum
patterns.howToSpot: A short sum/product whose angles pair to 90 degrees (35 & 55, 20 & 70...).
patterns.formula: $\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ-\theta)$ etc.; convert one of each pair and cancel.
patterns.logic:
1. List the angles; find the 90-degree pairs.
2. Convert the odd-pair function: $\sec 55^\circ = \frac{1}{\cos 55^\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 35^\circ}$.
3. Each term becomes $x \cdot \frac1x = 1$; read the sum.

Why: the exam numbers never share a function until you flip one — that flip is the entire question.

patterns.name: Product chains pairing to 1
patterns.howToSpot: Long products of tangents/cots at many small angles, with 45 in the middle or symmetric ends.
patterns.formula: $\tan\theta \cdot \tan(90^\circ - \theta) = 1$; pair from the ends inward.
patterns.logic:
1. Pair $\theta$ with $90^\circ - \theta$ from both ends.
2. Each pair contributes 1; any middle $\tan 45^\circ$ also contributes 1.
3. The product is 1 unless an unpaired angle remains — rare, and then it is stated.

Why: complementary tangents are reciprocals, so the chain self-destructs into a product of ones.

patterns.name: Finding the angle from complementary equality
patterns.howToSpot: 'If sin 3A = cos(A − 10), find A' — different functions at related angles, one unknown angle.
patterns.formula: Force the same function: $\cos x = \sin(90^\circ - x)$; then equate arguments. Shortcut: complementary arguments sum to 90.
patterns.logic:
1. Rewrite so both sides carry the same function.
2. Equate the arguments (or set them to sum to $90^\circ$ for complementary pairs).
3. Solve the resulting linear equation; verify the angle keeps every argument in range.

Why: equality of different functions is meaningless until one side is converted — then it is class-8 algebra.

patterns.name: Difference of complementary twins = 0
patterns.howToSpot: 'Find cos 50° − sin 40°' style — two terms that LOOK unrelated.
patterns.formula: $\sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta$: the two terms are identical; the difference is 0.
patterns.logic:
1. Check the arguments: $50 + 40 = 90$ → twins.
2. $\sin 40^\circ = \cos 50^\circ$; the expression is zero.
3. Same trick for $\cosec 68^\circ - \sec 22^\circ$, $\tan 81^\circ - \cot 9^\circ$.

Why: the question only wins if you don't check for the 90-degree sum — checking it ends the question instantly.

subtopics.title: Value-putting and given-ratio questions
subtopics.concept:
Two CGL workhorses:

1. **Given one ratio, draw the triangle.** If $\sin\theta=\frac{5}{13}$, take opposite $=5$, hypotenuse $=13$,
   adjacent $=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=12$ (a 5-12-13 triplet!) and read off every other ratio.
2. **Value-putting an identity.** If only $\sin\theta+\text{cosec}\theta$ or a quadratic condition like
   $\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ is given, convert the asked expression into the given pieces — or test a
   convenient $\theta$ when the expression is identically constant.

formulas.name: Sum-product of a ratio and reciprocal

tricks.title: Draw the triplet triangle
tricks.body: Ratio given → sides in hand in 5 seconds. Check the triplet table before any algebra.

tricks.title: Reduce the asked expression
tricks.body: Rewrite the target in terms of the given relation. For $x+\frac1x$ chains, square and subtract 2.

mistakes: Triplets applied with hypotenuse as a leg ($\sqrt{13^2-12^2}$ vs $\sqrt{13^2+12^2}$).
Forgetting that a given ratio fixes $\theta$ up to the quadrant — CGL keeps $\theta$ acute, so take the positive root.
Value-putting with $\theta=45^\circ$ when the expression is not constant — verify a second angle before trusting it.
subtopics.notes:
### Putting values into expressions
Two flavours: (a) the angle is a STANDARD one ($30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ$) — read the table and compute; (b) an angle satisfying a condition ("$\tan\theta = 2$") — reduce the expression to a single ratio, then substitute. Both end in one small fraction; the work is entirely in the reduction.
$$2\tan^2 45^\circ + \cos^2 30^\circ - \sin^2 60^\circ = 2 + \tfrac34 - \tfrac34 = 2$$

### The sin+cos condition web
Given $\sin\theta + \cos\theta = m$:
- $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{m^2 - 1}{2}$ (square the given).
- $\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \sqrt{2 - m^2}$ (from the difference squared).
- $\sin^3\theta + \cos^3\theta = m^3 - 3\sin\theta\cos\theta \cdot m$ via $x^3 + y^3 = (x+y)(x^2 - xy + y^2)$.
Special anchors: $m = \sqrt2$ gives $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac12$ ($\theta = 45^\circ$); $m = 1$ gives $\sin\theta\cos\theta = 0$ (endpoints).

### cot/tan triplet substitution
$\cot\theta = \frac{21}{20}$ means a 20-21-29 triangle: $\cos\theta = \frac{21}{29}$ directly. Any cot/tan given as a fraction of smallish integers is a triangle waiting to be drawn — faster than identities and immune to sign slips.

### Reducing linear fractions in sin and cos
$\frac{a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta}{c\cos\theta + d\sin\theta} \to \frac{a\tan\theta + b}{c + d\tan\theta}$ — divide by $\cos\theta$, substitute $t$, simplify. Works the same with $\cot$ if the expression is cot-heavy.

### The cosec/cot condition twin
Given $\cosec\theta + \cot\theta = k$: its conjugate $\cosec\theta - \cot\theta = \frac{1}{k}$ (product 1), so $\cosec\theta = \frac{k + \frac1k}{2}$ and $\cot\theta = \frac{k - \frac1k}{2}$. Since $\cosec^2 - \cot^2 = 1$, this family is the sec±tan engine wearing a different coat — and it finishes with $\sin\theta = \frac{2k}{k^2 + 1}$ directly. Example: $\cosec\theta + \cot\theta = 3$ gives $\cosec\theta = \frac{3 + \frac13}{2} = \frac53$, so $\sin\theta = \frac35$ — a 3-4-5 triangle in disguise.

### Reading the options like a setter
Options in this family are built from predictable slips: substituting the reciprocal of the given tan, forgetting the constant $+b$ term, dropping a minus sign when the denominator is negative, or reporting $\tan^2$ when $\tan$ was asked. After computing, name the slip each wrong option encodes — if you cannot, re-check your own arithmetic. And keep every substitution exact: $\tan\theta = \frac43$ stays a fraction; a decimal 1.33 is how sign and size errors sneak in.

### Quick revision
- Table entries at $0/30/45/60/90$; reduce everything to them.
- $\sin\cos = \frac{(\sin+\cos)^2 - 1}{2}$; $(\sin-\cos)^2 = 2 - (\sin+\cos)^2$.
- cot given as $\frac{p}{q}$ → triangle $(q, p, \sqrt{p^2+q^2})$.
- Divide linear fractions by $\cos\theta$; one substitution finishes them.

patterns.name: Standard angles in an expression
patterns.howToSpot: An arithmetic expression in sin/cos/tan of 0/30/45/60/90 asked as a single value.
patterns.formula: Substitute table values; simplify with exact fractions.
patterns.logic:
1. Replace each ratio with its table entry (reciprocal functions included).
2. Compute with fractions ($\frac14, \frac34, \frac12$) — no decimals.
3. Cancel before adding where possible.

Why: it is pure table recall plus one tidy computation — the marks are in avoiding the $\sin^2 60$ vs $\sin 60$ slips.

example.solution: $2(1) + \frac34 - \frac34 = 2$. The last two terms cancel exactly.

patterns.name: sin+cos given → products and differences
patterns.howToSpot: 'sinθ + cosθ = m' given; sinθcosθ, sinθ − cosθ, or a cubic combo asked.
patterns.formula: $\sin\cos = \frac{m^2-1}{2}$; $(\sin-\cos)^2 = 2 - m^2$; cube sums via $x^3+y^3 = (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2)$.
patterns.logic:
1. Square the given: $m^2 = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ → the product.
2. Difference: square root of $2 - m^2$ (positive since sin > cos or vice versa is possible — check signs only if options demand).
3. Cubes: factor as $(\sin + \cos)(1 - \sin\cos)$ and substitute both knowns.

Why: every quantity in this family is a symmetric function of $\sin$ and $\cos$ — the pair $(m, \sin\cos)$ determines all of them.

patterns.name: tan/cot condition into a linear fraction
patterns.howToSpot: 'If 5 tanθ = 4' or tanθ = p/q; a fraction like (5sinθ − 3cosθ)/(5sinθ + 3cosθ) asked.
patterns.formula: Divide by $\cos\theta$; the fraction becomes $\frac{5t - 3}{5t + 3}$ in $t = \tan\theta$.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert the condition to $t = \tan\theta$ first.
2. Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$.
3. Substitute and simplify the single fraction exactly.

Why: the coefficients of the question are the SAME numbers as in the fraction — substitution must be mechanical, not improvised.

patterns.name: cot/tan fraction → triangle → ratio
patterns.howToSpot: cotθ or tanθ given as a fraction like 21/20; a DIFFERENT ratio (cos, sin, sec) asked.
patterns.formula: Draw the triangle with legs $q, p$; hyp $= \sqrt{p^2+q^2}$; read the asked ratio.
patterns.logic:
1. $\cot\theta = \frac{21}{20}$ → adj 21, opp 20 → hyp 29.
2. Read the requested ratio from the same triangle.
3. Triplet families (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 20-21-29) cover the exams.

Why: the condition fully determines the shape — one drawing replaces three identity manipulations.

example.q: If $\cot\theta = \frac{21}{20}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\cos\theta$ is:

subtopics.title: Maximum and minimum values
subtopics.concept:
For $0^\circ\le\theta\le90^\circ$:
- $0\le\sin\theta,\cos\theta\le1$; $\sec\theta,\text{cosec}\theta\ge1$; $\tan\theta,\cot\theta$ are unbounded.
- $\sin\theta+\cos\theta\in[1,\sqrt2]$; $\sin\theta-\cos\theta\in[-1,1]$; $\sin\theta\cos\theta\le\frac12$.
- $a\sin^2\theta+b\cos^2\theta$ has minimum $\min(a,b)$ and maximum $\max(a,b)$.
- $a\tan^2\theta+b\cot^2\theta\ (\text{and } a\sin^2+b\,\text{cosec}^2)$ has minimum $2\sqrt{ab}$ by AM–GM.
- $\sec^2\theta+\text{cosec}^2\theta$ has minimum $2+2=4$ (at $45^\circ$).

tricks.title: Match the question to a range
tricks.body: Bounded pairs ($\sin+\cos$ etc.) → memorised range. Weighted square sums → min of coefficients or $2\sqrt{ab}$.

example.q: Find the minimum value of $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta$ for $0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$.

tricks.title: Weighted sin-cos squares are bounded by coefficients
tricks.body: $2\sin^2\theta+3\cos^2\theta=2+\cos^2\theta$, so it ranges from 2 to 3 — min 2, max 3, no calculus.

mistakes: AM-GM applied to $a\sin\theta+b\text{cosec}\theta$ where the equality point may be unreachable — for the square versions it is safe, check before using.
Quoting $\sqrt2$ as the **minimum** of $\sin+\cos$ — $\sqrt2$ is the maximum.
subtopics.notes:
### The amplitude formula (the workhorse)
For any angle $\theta$:
$$-\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \ \le\ a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta \ \le\ +\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$$
The maximum of $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ is $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and the minimum is its negative (unrestricted $\theta$); restricted to acute angles the range sits between the endpoint values — usually stated so the interior extremum is the answer. Instant values: $4\sin\theta + 3\cos\theta \to 5$, $5\sin\theta + 12\cos\theta \to 13$, $8\sin\theta - 15\cos\theta \to 17$ — Pythagorean pairs every time.
On $0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ$: $\sin\theta + \cos\theta$ ranges from $1$ to $\sqrt2$ — max $\sqrt2$ at $45^\circ$, min $1$ at the endpoints.

### The product bound
$$\sin\theta\cos\theta \le \frac12, \qquad 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta \le 1$$
Both maxima occur at $\theta = 45^\circ$. Any multiple $k\sin\theta\cos\theta$ peaks at $\frac{k}{2}$.

### Self-reciprocal sums (AM-GM)
$$\tan^2\theta + \cot^2\theta \ge 2,\qquad \sec^2\theta + \cosec^2\theta \ge 4,\qquad \tan\theta + \cot\theta \ge 2$$
All attained at $\theta = 45^\circ$. The $\sec^2 + \cosec^2$ version: $\frac{1}{\sin^2\cos^2} \ge 4$ since $\sin^2\cos^2 \le \frac14$. Any $x + \frac1x \ge 2$ shape with $x > 0$ follows the same rule, equality at $x = 1$.

### Ordering and comparison facts
On $(0^\circ, 90^\circ)$: $\sin$ rises $0 \to 1$, $\cos$ falls $1 \to 0$, $\tan$ rises $0 \to \infty$. So $\sin 60^\circ > \sin 45^\circ > \sin 30^\circ$; $\sin\theta > \cos\theta \iff \theta > 45^\circ$; $\tan\theta = \cot\theta$ only at $45^\circ$. Also $\frac{1}{1+\sin^2\theta}$ is smallest when $\sin^2\theta$ is largest ($= 1$), giving minimum $\frac12$.

### The 45° equality case and restricted domains
Every bound in this block is attained at $\theta = 45^\circ$: the amplitude expressions reach $\pm\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ only for unrestricted $\theta$ (the peak of $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ sits at $\tan\theta = \frac{a}{b}$, which is acute for positive $a, b$ — so on $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ the max $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ IS reachable, while the negative minimum is cut off at the endpoint $-b$). Always read the domain: "for all $\theta$" allows the negative amplitude; "$0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ$" floors the minimum at the endpoint value. Options often include both — the domain decides.

### Quick revision
- $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$: max $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, min $-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
- $\sin\theta\cos\theta \le \frac12$; $2\sin\theta\cos\theta \le 1$, both at $45^\circ$.
- $\tan^2 + \cot^2 \ge 2$; $\sec^2 + \cosec^2 \ge 4$; $x + \frac1x \ge 2$ with equality at $x=1$.
- $\sin$ up, $\cos$ down on $(0^\circ, 90^\circ)$; crossover at $45^\circ$.

patterns.name: Max/min of a sinθ ± b cosθ
patterns.howToSpot: 'Find the maximum of 4sinθ + 3cosθ' — a linear combination with Pythagorean coefficients.
patterns.formula: Max $= +\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, min $= -\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ for $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$.
patterns.logic:
1. Read off $(a, b)$; compute $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ — expect a triplet.
2. Maximum positive, minimum negative (unless $\theta$ is restricted; then check endpoints).
3. Quote both if 'range' is asked.

Why: the expression is a single wave with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ — the formula IS the answer.

patterns.name: Bounds of sinθ cosθ
patterns.howToSpot: Max/min of sinθcosθ or 2sinθcosθ (sometimes with a coefficient or a plus-one).
patterns.formula: $\sin\theta\cos\theta \le \frac12$; $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin2\theta \le 1$; both peak at $45^\circ$.
patterns.logic:
1. Recognise the product form; halve the coefficient for the max of $k\sin\theta\cos\theta$.
2. Or convert to $\sin 2\theta$ and use the wave range.
3. Minimum on acute angles is $0$ (endpoint); quote only if asked.

Why: the product is the double-angle formula in disguise — one conversion bounds it.

example.q: The maximum value of $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:

patterns.name: AM-GM self-reciprocal sums
patterns.howToSpot: Minimum of tan²+cot², sec²+cosec², tan+cot — or an equation whose sum equals the bound.
patterns.formula: $x + \frac1x \ge 2$; $\sec^2\theta + \cosec^2\theta = \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta} \ge 4$.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the self-reciprocal pair; quote the AM-GM bound.
2. $\sec^2 + \cosec^2$: combine to $\frac{1}{\sin^2\cos^2}$, then use $\sin\cos \le \frac12$.
3. Equality case: $\theta = 45^\circ$ in every one of these.

Why: reciprocal pairs cannot be small simultaneously — the product $x \cdot \frac1x = 1$ forces the sum up.

patterns.name: Ordering and crossover comparisons
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is largest: sin 30, sin 45, sin 60?'; 'sinθ > cosθ for which θ?'; minimum of 1/(1+sin²θ).
patterns.formula: On $(0^\circ, 90^\circ)$: sin increases, cos decreases; crossover at $45^\circ$; denominators largest → fraction smallest.
patterns.logic:
1. Monotonicity orders same-function comparisons instantly.
2. sin vs cos comparisons pivot at $45^\circ$.
3. For $\frac{1}{1+\sin^2\theta}$: minimise by maximising the denominator ($\sin^2\theta = 1$).

Why: the monotone staircase of the three functions on the acute quadrant decides everything without computation.

example.solution: $\theta > 45^\circ$ — the crossover of the two graphs is at $45^\circ$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sum/difference/product of sin/cos/tan (often sec/cosec/cot too) at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° asked as one value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert every function to its table value via the $\frac{\sqrt{k}}{2}$ construction (reciprocals for sec/cosec/cot), then compute with exact fractions. Keep surds as surds; rationalise only the final answer.

pyqPatterns.pattern: One ratio given → the rest of the triangle
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'If sinθ = 3/5 find tanθ' style — one ratio (sometimes surd form), other ratios asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Draw the right triangle from the given ratio, complete the third side by Pythagoras (expect a triplet), and read the asked ratio off the same triangle w.r.t. the named angle.

example.q: If $\cosec\theta = \frac{13}{5}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'If secθ + tanθ = m, find secθ − tanθ' — or the pair subtracted/added to extract an individual ratio.
pyqPatterns.approach: $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)(\sec\theta - \tan\theta) = 1$, so the conjugate is its reciprocal $\frac{1}{m}$. Adding/subtracting the pair gives $2\sec\theta$ and $2\tan\theta$ individually; a triangle then returns sin/cos.

example.q: If $\cosec\theta + \cot\theta = 3$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\cosec\theta - \cot\theta$ is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sum (or difference) of sin and cos given as m; the product sinθcosθ, the opposite difference, or a cubic combination asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Square the given: $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{m^2-1}{2}$; $(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 = 2 - m^2$; cubes via $x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2)$. Sub-specials: $m = \sqrt2$ → product $\frac12$; $m = 1$ → product $0$.

pyqPatterns.pattern: tanθ given → linear fraction in sin and cos
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: tanθ = p/q (or 5tanθ = 4 style); a fraction like (a·sinθ + b·cosθ)/(c·cosθ + d·sinθ) asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$: the fraction becomes $\frac{a\tan\theta + b}{c + d\tan\theta}$. Substitute $t = \frac{p}{q}$ exactly (fractions, not decimals) and simplify once.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Angles pair to 90° (35 & 55, 20 & 70...) across different functions — or a long tangent chain with 45° in the middle.
pyqPatterns.approach: Flip one function of each pair: $\sec 55^\circ = \frac{1}{\sin 35^\circ}$ etc.; products like $\tan\theta\tan(90^\circ-\theta) = 1$. Chains $\tan 1^\circ \cdots \tan 89^\circ$ collapse to 1. Difference-of-twins questions ($\cos 50^\circ - \sin 40^\circ$) are instantly 0.

example.solution: Pairs: $10+80 = 90$ and $20+70 = 90$; each pair multiplies to 1, so the product is 1.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'If sin 3A = cos(A − 10°), find A' — different functions at related angles, one unknown.
pyqPatterns.approach: Force the same function ($\cos x = \sin(90^\circ - x)$) or use the shortcut: complementary-function arguments sum to $90^\circ$. Solve the resulting linear equation; sanity-check the angle keeps all arguments in range.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the maximum of 4sinθ + 3cosθ' — Pythagorean coefficients; minimum may be asked instead.
pyqPatterns.approach: Max $= +\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, min $= -\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ (unrestricted θ); with $0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ$ check endpoints too. Expect triplets: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Minimum of tan²+cot², sec²+cosec², tan+cot — or the max of sinθcosθ / 2sinθcosθ.

example.q: The minimum value of $\tan\theta + \cot\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:

pyqPatterns.pattern: Two sides of the right triangle → a named ratio
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two sides given (or hyp + one leg); sin/cos/tan of one acute angle asked — the angle described in words ('opposite the longer leg').
pyqPatterns.approach: Third side by Pythagoras, then attach opposite/adjacent to the NAMED angle — 'opposite the shorter leg' is the smaller angle. Triplet multiples supply the exam numbers.

example.q: In a right triangle, the legs adjacent to and opposite an acute angle are $15$ cm and $8$ cm. The hypotenuse is:

solvedExamples.shortcut: Recognise the form: $\frac{2t}{1-t^2}=\tan2\theta$ with $\theta=30^\circ$ → $\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3$, no fractions at all.

solvedExamples.q: If $\cos\theta=\dfrac{7}{25}$, then the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: see 7 and 25, write 24 instantly. Trap: $\frac{7}{24}$ is $\cot\theta$.

solvedExamples.solution:
Pair $\tan\theta$ with $\tan(90^\circ-\theta)=\cot\theta$: each pair multiplies to 1.

44 such pairs plus $\tan45^\circ=1$ give the product 1.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Every angle pairs with its complement; middle term is $\tan45^\circ=1$. Product $=1$.
Reduce each bracket to a single fraction; the $\sin^2\cos^2$ cancels completely → 1. (Check at $45^\circ$: $(\frac{1}{\sqrt2})^2\times2=1$.)

solvedExamples.solution:
$a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta$ peaks at $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$: here $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ (at $\tan\theta=\frac34$).

So the greatest value of the expression is $5+5=10$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=5$ for the trig part, then add the constant: $5+5=10$. Trap: 12 (added $3+4+5$ directly).
solvedExamples.pattern: max of a sin + b cos + c

practice.shortcut: Read the table: $\frac12+\frac12+1=2$. $\cot45^\circ=1$, not 0.
$\sec^2-\tan^2=1$ (identity pair), then $1-\sin^2=\cos^2$.
This is $\sin(60+30)=\sin90^\circ=1$ — recognise the sine-addition shape instead of multiplying.
5-12-13 triplet → $\frac{5}{12}$. Trap: $\frac{12}{5}$ is $\cot\theta$.
Divide through by $\cos\theta$: $(t+1)/(t-1)$ with $t=\frac34$ → $-7$. (Same trick works for any sin/cos ratio expression.)
practice.pattern: divide by cos to use tan

practice.q: If $\sin(40^\circ+\theta)=\cos(30^\circ+\theta)$, where both angles are acute, then $\theta$ equals:
practice.shortcut: Sum to 90: $70+2\theta=90$ → $\theta=10^\circ$. Trap: 20 (forgot to halve).
practice.pattern: sin A = cos B angle equation

practice.q: If $\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$, then the value of $\cos^2\theta+\cos^4\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
From the condition, $\sin^2\theta=1-\sin\theta$, so $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta=\sin\theta$.

Then $\cos^4\theta=\sin^2\theta=1-\sin\theta$.

Sum $=\sin\theta+1-\sin\theta=1$.
practice.shortcut: $\cos^2=\sin$ and $\cos^4=\sin^2=1-\sin$ → total 1, without ever finding $\theta$.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ for $0^\circ\le\theta\le90^\circ$ is:
practice.solution: $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ ranges from 1 (at $\theta=0^\circ$ or $90^\circ$) to $\sqrt2$ (at $45^\circ$). The minimum is 1.
practice.shortcut: Range $[1,\sqrt2]$: min 1, max $\sqrt2$. Trap: $\sqrt2$ is the **maximum**.
Complementary pairs collapse; $\tan45^\circ=1$ stands alone.
The $s^2c^2$ terms cancel exactly: $-6+6=0$ → answer 0 for every $\theta$. (Try $\theta=45^\circ$ to confirm.)
5-12-13: $\sin=\frac5{13}$ → cosec $=\frac{13}{5}$ (flip). Trap: $\frac{13}{12}$ is $\sec\theta$.

practice.q: The minimum value of $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta$ (for acute $\theta$) is:
practice.solution:
By AM–GM, $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta\ge2\sqrt{4\times9}=12$,

with equality when $2\tan\theta=3\cot\theta$, i.e. $\tan^2\theta=\frac32$ (reachable since tan is unbounded).
practice.shortcut: $2\sqrt{ab}=2\sqrt{36}=12$. Trap: 6 is $\sqrt{ab}$ (forgot to double), 13 is $a+b$.
Companion is $\frac1k=\frac13$; average the pair: cosec $=\frac{3+\frac13}{2}=\frac53$ → $\sin=\frac35$.

practice.solution:
Write the brackets as $[t+(s-1)][t-(s-1)]=t^2-(s-1)^2$ where $t=\tan\theta$, $s=\sec\theta$.

$=t^2-s^2+2s-1=-1+2s-1=2(\sec\theta-1)$, using $s^2-t^2=1$.
practice.shortcut: Difference of squares, then $t^2-s^2=-1$: answer $2(\sec\theta-1)$. Quick check at $30^\circ$: LHS $\approx0.309$ = RHS.

practice.solution:
Write the left side as $2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)+5\cos^2\theta=2+5\cos^2\theta$.

So $2+5\cos^2\theta=6\Rightarrow\cos^2\theta=\frac45$, hence $\sin^2\theta=\frac15$.

$\tan^2\theta=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}=\frac{1/5}{4/5}=\frac14\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\frac12$ (acute).
practice.shortcut: Anchor to $a(\sin^2+\cos^2)+(b-a)\cos^2$: solve for $\cos^2$, then $\tan^2=\frac{1-\cos^2}{\cos^2}$. Traps: 2 (reciprocal), $\frac14$ ($\tan^2$, forgot the root).
Complementary twins: both read $\frac{\sqrt1}{2}$. Trap: $\frac12$ (evaluating only one term).
$1 + 1 - 1 = 1$. Trap: $2$ (forgetting the coefficient is already consumed).
Both terms are $\sqrt3$. Trap: $\sqrt3$ (assuming they cancel or one is $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$).

practice.q: If $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\tan = \frac{3}{4}$. Trap: $\frac43$ (tan of the OTHER acute angle).

practice.q: If $\cos\theta = \frac{12}{13}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta - \tan\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{13}{12} - \frac{5}{12} = \frac23$. Trap: $\frac{5}{12}$ — that is $\tan\theta$ itself.

practice.q: If $\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\cosec^2\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\cosec^2 = 1 + \cot^2 = 1 + 7 = 8$ — the identity does it in one line. Trap: $\sqrt8$ (forgot to square).

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$ right-angled at $B$, $AB = 5$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. The value of $\sin A$ is:
practice.solution: AC $= \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$. Side opposite to $A$ is $BC = 12$: $\sin A = \frac{12}{13}$.
practice.shortcut: Opposite to A is BC, not AB. Trap: $\frac{5}{13}$ (reading the wrong leg as opposite).

practice.q: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is $25$ cm and one leg is $7$ cm. The cosine of the angle opposite the $7$ cm leg is:
practice.solution:
Third leg $= \sqrt{625 - 49} = 24$ (7-24-25). The angle opposite $7$ has adjacent leg $24$:

$\cos = \frac{24}{25}$.
practice.shortcut: Opposite 7 → adjacent is 24 → $\cos = \frac{24}{25}$. Trap: $\frac{7}{25}$ (that is the SINE of the same angle).
$2 + 2 = 4$. Trap: $2$ (assuming the two terms cancel or equal 1).

practice.solution:
$\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1$ for every $\theta$ where defined — the answer is $1$ without any table work.

(Indeed $\sec^2 30^\circ = \frac43$, $\tan^2 30^\circ = \frac13$.)
practice.shortcut: The identity $\sec^2 - \tan^2 = 1$ is angle-independent. Trap: $\frac13$ — computing entries and slipping.

practice.q: If $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 5$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta - \tan\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: Conjugate = reciprocal: $\frac15$. Trap: $4$ (subtracting instead of using the product).

practice.q: If $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 5$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
Subtract the conjugate: $2\tan\theta = 5 - \frac15 = \frac{24}{5}$ → $\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5}$.

(5-12-13 triangle: $\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}$ if ever asked.)
practice.shortcut: $\tan = \frac{m - 1/m}{2} = \frac{12}{5}$. Trap: $\frac{5}{12}$ — the inverse fraction.
Cross terms cancel: $2$. Trap: $1$ (using $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ and forgetting the second bracket).
Convert all three, cancel to $1$. Trap: $0$ (assuming one bracket vanishes — none does).
$\frac{4t - 1}{4 + t} = \frac{8}{19}$. Trap: $\frac{8}{13}$ (using $t = \frac34$ as $t = \frac43$).
$\frac{2t+1}{t-2} = 7$. Trap: $-7$ — a sign slip reading $t - 2$ as $2 - t$.
$\tan = 1$ at $45^\circ$ only. Trap: $90^\circ$ (where $\sin = 1$, $\cos = 0$ — not equal).

practice.q: If $\sin\theta + \cosec\theta = 2$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sin^2\theta + \cosec^2\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: The sum 2 forces $\sin\theta = 1$: both squares are 1. Trap: $4$ (squaring the given sum).
Squaring $s^2 + c^2 = 1$ is the whole proof. Trap: $1$ — true only when one function is zero.

practice.solution:
Cube the identity: $(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta)^3 = 1$ expands to

$\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta + 3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta = 1$, so the sum is $1 - 3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$.
practice.shortcut: $x^3 + y^3 = (x+y)^3 - 3xy(x+y)$ with $x+y = 1$. Trap: $1 - 2s^2c^2$ — that is the FOURTH-power form.

practice.q: If $\tan\theta + \cot\theta = 2$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
$x + \frac1x = 2$ forces $x = 1$ (a positive number and its reciprocal sum to 2 only at equality).

So $\tan\theta = 1$, i.e. $\theta = 45^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $x + \frac{1}{x} \ge 2$ with equality only at $x = 1$. Trap: $2$ (confusing the sum with the value).

practice.q: If $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac{1}{3}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: Average the pair: $\frac{3 + \frac13}{2} = \frac53$. Trap: $\frac{10}{3}$ (forgot to halve).
Twins cancel. Trap: $1$ or $\frac12$ — treating them as unrelated values.
Both flip to reciprocals: $1 + 1 = 2$. Trap: $1$ (cancelling only one pair).
$22 + 68 = 90$: identical twins. Trap: $\sec 22^\circ$ (dropping the second term).
Pair the ends: $1$. Trap: $0$ — nothing here is zero; every factor is finite and positive.
Two pairs: $1 \times 1 = 1$. Trap: $\frac{1}{3}$ (squaring the 30-60 pair instead of multiplying).
$4A = 100$: $A = 25^\circ$. Trap: $20^\circ$ (dropping the $-10^\circ$).

practice.solution:
$\sec x = \cosec(90^\circ - x)$: the arguments must satisfy $2\theta + \theta + 30^\circ = 90^\circ$.

$3\theta = 60^\circ$ → $\theta = 20^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $3\theta = 60$: $\theta = 20^\circ$. Trap: $30^\circ$ (setting $2\theta = \theta + 30$, the wrong pairing).
$2\theta = 60$: $\theta = 30^\circ$. Trap: $45^\circ$ (tan $=$ cot only at 45 when the angles are EQUAL, not complementary).

practice.solution:
Pair $1^\circ$ with $89^\circ$, $2^\circ$ with $88^\circ$, ..., $44^\circ$ with $46^\circ$: 44 pairs each multiplying to 1.

$\tan 45^\circ = 1$ remains in the middle. Product $= 1$.
practice.shortcut: 44 cancelling pairs + $\tan 45^\circ$: product $1$. Trap: $0$ — no factor is zero (tan 0 is absent).

practice.solution:
Complementary cots are reciprocals: $\cot 15^\circ \cot 75^\circ = 1$ (since $15 + 75 = 90$) and $\cot 35^\circ \cot 55^\circ = 1$.

Product $= 1$.
practice.shortcut: Pairs $(15, 75)$ and $(35, 55)$: $1 \times 1 = 1$. Trap: assuming cot-cot pairs don't cancel — complementary cots are still reciprocals.

practice.solution:
$27 + 63 = 90$ and $35 + 55 = 90$: both pairs multiply to 1; $\tan 45^\circ = 1$.

Product $= 1$.
practice.shortcut: Two complementary pairs + the 45° anchor: $1$. Trap: $0$ — no factor vanishes.

practice.solution:
$\sin 76^\circ = \cos 14^\circ$ and $\sin 59^\circ = \cos 31^\circ$ (each pair sums to $90^\circ$).

So the sum $= (\sin^2 14^\circ + \cos^2 14^\circ) + (\sin^2 31^\circ + \cos^2 31^\circ) = 1 + 1 = 2$.
practice.shortcut: Re-pair into two $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ groups. Trap: $1$ — there are TWO independent pairs here.
Complementary squares cancel. Trap: $3$ (using $\sin^2 60 = \frac34$ for BOTH terms wrongly) or $\frac32$.
$\frac14 + \frac14 + 1 = \frac32$. Trap: $2$ — counting $\tan^2 45^\circ$ twice.
$\frac{m^2 - 1}{2} = \frac12$. Trap: $1$ (forgetting to divide by 2).
$\sqrt{2 - 2} = 0$: at $45^\circ$ the difference vanishes. Trap: $1$ (using $2 - m$ instead of $2 - m^2$).
$\frac{5t - 3}{5t + 3} = \frac{1}{7}$. Trap: $\frac12$ (substituting $t = \frac54$ upside down).
$\frac{3t+1}{t+3} = \frac75$. Trap: $\frac57$ — inverting the final fraction.

practice.q: If $\cot\theta = \frac{21}{20}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\cos\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{21}{29}$. Trap: $\frac{20}{29}$ — that is $\sin\theta$ (cot's numerator is the ADJACENT side).

practice.q: If $\tan\theta = \frac{4}{3}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac53$. Trap: $\frac35$ — sec is hyp/ADJ, not adj/hyp.

practice.q: If $\sin\theta - \cos\theta = 0$ and $\theta$ is acute, the value of $\sin\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $45^\circ$: $\sin = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$. Trap: $1$ (that is $\sin 90^\circ$).
$\frac{2t - 1}{2 + 3t} = \frac{3}{22}$. Trap: $\frac{22}{3}$ — the fraction inverted.

practice.solution:
$(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 = 2 - \left(\frac75\right)^2 = 2 - \frac{49}{25} = \frac{1}{25}$.

So $\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \frac15$ (positive root for the acute $\theta$ in the standard exam setup).
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt{2 - m^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{25}} = \frac15$. Trap: $\frac{7}{5}$ — that is the given sum itself.
$\sqrt{25} = 5$. Trap: $7$ (adding the coefficients) or $\sqrt7$ (adding squares without the root).

practice.q: The minimum value of $5\sin\theta + 12\cos\theta$ (for all $\theta$) is:
practice.shortcut: $-\sqrt{169} = -13$. Trap: $13$ (forgetting the minus on the minimum).

practice.q: For $0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ$, the maximum value of $\sin\theta + \cos\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
$(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \le 1 + 1 = 2$, so the max is $\sqrt2$ at $45^\circ$.

(Or: amplitude of the combination is $\sqrt{1^2+1^2} = \sqrt2$.)
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt{1+1} = \sqrt2$ at $45^\circ$. Trap: $2$ (adding the individual maxima — they occur at different angles).

practice.q: The maximum value of $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac12$ at $45^\circ$. Trap: $1$ — that is the max of $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, not of the product.
$\sin 90^\circ = 1$ via the double angle. Trap: $\frac12$ — halving twice.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\tan^2\theta + \cot^2\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $2$ at $45^\circ$. Trap: $0$ — a positive term and its reciprocal cannot both vanish.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\sec^2\theta + \cosec^2\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{1}{(\sin\cos)^2} \ge 4$. Trap: $2$ — the bound for $\tan^2 + \cot^2$, not this pair.

practice.q: Which of the following is the largest?
practice.shortcut: $\sin 60^\circ$. Trap: $\cos 60^\circ = \sin 30^\circ$ — they tie at $0.5$, well below $\sin 45^\circ$.

practice.solution: $\sin$ rises and $\cos$ falls; they cross at $45^\circ$. Beyond it, $\sin$ is on top.
practice.shortcut: $\theta > 45^\circ$. Trap: $<$ — the directions of the two functions are easy to swap.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\frac{1}{1 + \sin^2\theta}$ ($\theta$ real) is:
practice.solution:
The fraction is smallest when the denominator is largest: $\sin^2\theta = 1$ gives $1 + 1 = 2$.

Minimum $= \frac12$.
practice.shortcut: $\frac12$ at $\theta = 90^\circ$. Trap: $0$ — the fraction never reaches zero since $1 + \sin^2 \ge 1 > 0$.

practice.q: The minimum value of $8\sin\theta - 15\cos\theta$ over all real $\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
Amplitude $= \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = \sqrt{289} = 17$; the expression ranges over $[-17, 17]$.

Minimum $= -17$.
practice.shortcut: $-\sqrt{64 + 225} = -17$. Trap: $17$ (missing the minus) or $-7$ (subtracting the coefficients).

practice.q: The minimum value of $9\tan^2\theta + 4\cot^2\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $2\sqrt{9 \times 4} = 12$. Trap: $13$ ($a + b$) or $6$ ($\sqrt{ab}$, forgot to double).
